 HON'BLE DR. JUSTICE PUSHPENDRA SINGH BHATI HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE MUNNURI LAXMAN Judgment 27/09/2024 Per Dr. Pushpendra Singh Bhati, J:
1.
The instant Criminal Appeal No.336/1997 under Section 378 of the Cr.P.C.

has been preferred by the appellant-State and the present Criminal Revision Petition 83/1997 has been preferred by complainant-Chunnilal, laying a challenge to the common judgment of acquittal dated 29.11.1996 passed by the learned District and Sessions Judge, Bikaner in the Sessions Case No. 39/95 (State of Rajasthan v. Tejmal and others), whereby the accused-respondents were acquitted of the charges against them [2024:RJ-JD:41780-DB] (2 of 15) [CRLA-336/1997] under Sections 498A, 302 r/w 34, 304B r/w 34 and 306 r/w 34 of the IPC.

entities.text: Chuni Lal vs Tejmaal And Ors (2024:Rj-Jd:41780-Db)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The matters pertains to an incident which has occurred in the year 1995 and the present appeal as well as Revision Petition have been pending since the year 1997.

3. At the outset, the learned GA cum AAG appearing on behalf of the State has produced before this Court a communication dated 21.08.2024 received from the Police Station, Napasar, District Bikaner, wherein it has been recorded that accused-respondent Smt. Durga w/o Tikuram has already expired.
The said report is taken on record.
3.1. Thus, the present appeal and revision petition qua the deceased accused respondent Smt. Durga is dismissed as abated.

3.2. In this view of the matter, the present appeal and revision petition is surviving only qua accused-respondents (surviving), namely, Tejmal, Jagmala Ram and Smt. Saroj,
and the present adjudication is being made accordingly.

4. Brief facts of the case, as placed before the Court by Mr. N.K. Gurjar, learned GA cum AAG appearing on behalf of the appellant- State, are that on 04.04.1995, the complainant-Chunni Lal (PW1) lodged a written report before the Police Station Napasar, District Bikaner that in the year 1989, his daughter Tara Devi (deceased, herein) was married to Tejmal, son of Teku Ram; at the time of marriage, dowry was given to the husband of the complainant's daughter (deceased).
But his daughter Tara Devi reported from time to time that she was tortured by her husband's family.
According to the complainant, on 07.03.1995, the deceased came to the complainant and told that her husband and mother- in-law demanded Rs.20,000/- from her.
The complainant pacified her and told her not to worry and go back home.
On 01.04.1995, at around 1:00 p.m., the complainant's son, Moolchand (PW6) came to him and informed the complainant that Tara Devi has died due to burn injuries.

Upon hearing this,
the complainant and his elder brother reached Belasar village and found Tara Devi's body lying in a room.
It was informed that in-laws of the deceased, were not present at the place of incident at the relevant time.
5. On the basis of the aforementioned information, an FIR was registered and the investigation commenced accordingly.
After investigation, the police filed a charge-sheet against the accused- respondents.
The learned Trial Court framed the charges against the accused-respondents under Sections 498A, 302/34 in alteration Sections 304B and 306 IPC.
The charges were read over to the accused-respondents, which they denied and claimed to stand the trial and the trial commenced accordingly.

6. During the course of trial, the prosecution produced witnesses PW-1 to PW-11 and got exhibited documents Ex.P-1 to Ex.P-10A; and in defence, witnesses DW 1 and DW2 were examined on behalf of the accused-respondents; whereafter, the accused- respondents examined under Section 313 CrPC, wherein the accused respondents pleaded innocence and their false implication in the criminal case in question.

[2024:RJ-JD:41780-DB] (4 of 15) [CRLA-336/1997]
Chuni Lal vs Tejmaal And Ors (2024:Rj-Jd:41780-Db) on 27 September, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/61538477/
2 7.

entities.text: Chuni Lal vs Tejmaal And Ors (2024:Rj-Jd:41780-Db)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Thereafter, upon hearing the contentions of both the parties as well as considering the material and evidence placed on record, the learned Trial Court, acquitted the accused-respondents, vide the impugned judgment of acquittal dated 29.11.1996, against which the present appeal and revision petition has been preferred on the behalf of the appellant-State as well as the petitioner- complainant.

8. Learned GA cum AAG appearing on behalf of the State submits that in the present case, the death in question was caused otherwise than under normal circumstances, within seven years of the deceased's marriage and it became clear from the testimony of the complainant (PW1) that his daughter (deceased) was subjected to cruelty by her husband and his relatives in connection with the demand of dowry and therefore in the instant case, all the essential ingredients of Section 304B IPC are made out.
8.1.

Learned counsel further submits that with regard to the issue concerning delay in lodging of FIR, a certain amount of delay is plausible on the part of the family members when such a grave event occurs.
Moreover, the same has been well explained in the instant case as well, thereby making such a delay worthy of being condoned.

8.2. Learned counsel also submits that in the given factual matrix, the prosecution has been able to successfully establish the chain of circumstances, commencing from the date of marriage wherein the dowry was given, to the penultimate event, wherein the deceased went to her parents' house to inform them about the [2024:RJ-JD:41780-DB] (5 of 15) [CRLA-336/1997] death-threats which she was receiving in connection to the dowry demand from her in-laws, to the ultimate act of setting her on fire after pouring kerosene.

9. On the other hand, Ms. Shreshtha Mathur, learned Amicus Curiae appearing for the accused-respondents, while opposing the aforesaid submissions made on behalf of the appellant-State, submits that the postmortem report indicated no mark of injury other than burn injuries on the body of the deceased, which in turn indicates, absence of any signs of mental or physical harassment, being meted out to the deceased by her in-laws.

9.1. Learned counsel further submits that the delay in lodging of the FIR is detrimental to the prosecution case, as no satisfactory explanation has been given by the complainant, Chunni Lal (PW1) in regard to such delay.

9.2. Learned counsel also submits that most of the prosecution witnesses, especially, PW1, PW2,
PW4, PW6 and PW7 are relatives of the deceased, and therefore, in the absence of any independent witnesses, their testimony is not reliable.

In this regard, reliance was placed upon the judgment rendered by the Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Shoor Singh and Anr. v. State of Uttarakhand,
(Criminal Appeal No. 249 of 2013, decided on 20.09.2024).

entities.text:
Shoor Singh and Anr. v. State of Uttarakhand,
(Criminal Appeal No. 249 of 2013
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 9.3. Learned counsel further submits that most of the prosecution witnesses have testified the absence of any contentious or disputed relationship between the deceased and accused- respondent (husband), and therefore, there were no prevalent signs or background of marital discord to explain motive, on part [2024:RJ-JD:41780-DB] (6 of 15) [CRLA-336/1997] of the accused-respondent, for commission of the crime in question.

Chuni Lal vs Tejmaal And Ors (2024:Rj-Jd:41780-Db) on 27 September, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/61538477/
3 9.4.

entities.text: Chuni Lal vs Tejmaal And Ors (2024:Rj-Jd:41780-Db)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
Learned counsel also submits that presumption under Section 113-B of the Indian Evidence Act,
1872 arises only when the necessary ingredients of a dowry death are proved beyond all reasonable doubts.

However, in the present case there are no direct or reliable evidence to establish that the victim (deceased) was subjected to cruelty in connection with demand of dowry soon before her death by the accused-respondents and therefore there was no occasion in the present factual matrix to raise a presumption in respect of dowry death.

9.5. Learned counsel further submits that the subsequent conduct of the accused-respondents has also been reasonable as evident from the factum that the accused-respondent husband's younger brother only informed the police about the death in question.

9.6. Learned counsel also submits that the accused-respondents and other family members were not present at the crime scene, at the relevant time, which in absence of any direct evidence indicating instigation or involvement of the accused-respondents in commission of the crime in question, puts the present case to the test of circumstantial evidence and in absence of any cogent evidence indicating towards marital discord and a weak chain of circumstantial evidences, inclines the case in the favour of the accused-respondents.

9.7. Learned counsel further submits that an appellate Court, must bear in mind that in case of acquittal, two reasonable conclusions are possible on the basis of the evidence on record;
[2024:RJ-JD:41780-DB] (7 of 15) [CRLA-336/1997] ordinarily, the Appellate Court should not disturb the finding of acquittal recorded by the Trial Court.

In this regard, reliance was placed on the judgment rendered by the Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Chandrappa and Ors. v. State of Karnataka (2007) 4 SCC 415.
10.

entities.text: Chandrappa and Ors. v. State of Karnataka (2007) 4 SCC 415
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Heard learned counsel for the parties as well as perused the record of the case, along with the judgments cited at the Bar.

11. This Court observes that the accused-respondents were charged with the offence of dowry death and after conducting the trial, learned Trial Court acquitted them of the charges under Sections 498A, 302 r/w 34, 304B r/w 34 and 306 r/w 34 of IPC, vide the impugned judgment.

12. This Court further observes that as per the evidence available on record in the present case, there were no eye witnesses to the incident in question, and that the family members of the deceased were informed about her death, only after she died due to burns.
Therefore, the guilt of the accused-respondents in the present case, lies solely upon the circumstantial evidences.

12.1. In this regard, this Court is conscious of the judgment rendered in the case of Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v.
State of Maharashtra (1984) 4 SCC 116, wherein the Hon'ble Apex Court laid down the five golden principles, which constitute the Panch-Sheel of the proof of a case based on circumstantial evidence,
as follows:
(1) The circumstances from which the conclusion of guilt is to be drawn should be fully established.

entities.text:
Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v.
State of Maharashtra (1984) 4 SCC 116
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It may be noted here that this Court indicated that the circumstances concerned 'must or should' and not 'may be' established.

Chuni Lal vs Tejmaal And Ors (2024:Rj-Jd:41780-Db) on 27 September, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/61538477/
4 [2024:RJ-JD:41780-DB] (8 of 15) [CRLA-336/1997] There is not only a grammatical but a legal distinction between 'may be proved' and 'must be or should be proved' as was held by this Court in Shivaji Sahabrao Bobade & Anr. v. State of Maharashtra where the following observations were made: "Certainly, it is a primary principle that the accused must be and not merely may be guilty before a court can convict and the mental distance between 'may be' and 'must be' is long and divides vague conjectures from sure conclusions."

entities.text: Chuni Lal vs Tejmaal And Ors (2024:Rj-Jd:41780-Db)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

entities.text: Shivaji Sahabrao Bobade & Anr. v. State of Maharashtra
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
(2) The facts so established should be consistent only with the hypothesis of the guilt of the accused,
that is to say.

they should not be explainable on any other hypothesis except that the accused is guilty, (3) the circumstances should be of a conclusive nature and tendency, (4) they should exclude every possible hypothesis except the one to be proved, and (5) there must be a chain of evidence so complete as not to leave any reasonable ground for the conclusion consistent with the innocence of the accused and must show that in all human probability, the act must have been done by the accused."

13. This Court also observes that the action of the accused- respondents as soon as the incident in question happened, of immediately sending Hanuman (PW5) to report the incident in question to the concerned police authorities, which is even corroborated by the testimonies of Premsukh (PW9)
and Ratnaram (PW4)
, plausibly manifests the absence of any desirability to concoct or hide the evidence relating to the incident.
Additionally, the accused-respondents also informed about the same to the family of the deceased as is testified by the Moolchandra (PW6).

14. This Court further observes that the incident took place on 01.04.1995 and the FIR was registered on 04.04.1995, and [2024:RJ-JD:41780-DB] (9 of 15) [CRLA-336/1997] therefore, there has been an unexplained delay of 3 days in lodging of the FIR, which hints towards premeditation on part of the family of the deceased in the framing of the contents of the complaint.

This Court also observes that the aforesaid unexplained delay is corroborated by the testimony of Chunnilal (PW1)
who admitted that the report (Ex.P-1) was written by his son and there is no explanation in the FIR as to why this report was filed belatedly.

It was further admitted by Ratanaram (PW4) that he got the written report drafted by an Advocate Shri Sahak and the same hints towards premeditation and resort to legal advice, calculated to implicate the accused-respondents successfully.

15. This Court further observes that statement of the witnesses PW 1 (Chunnilal), PW 4 (Ratnaram),
PW 6 (Moolchand), PW 7 (Jugal Kishore) under Section 161 Cr.P.C. were also recorded by the police after 12 days of the incident in question, and there has been no explanation for the said delay, which is considered as fatal for the prosecution's case.
16.

This Court also observes that father of the deceased i.e., PW1 (Chunnilal) stated in his testimony that there was no talk regarding giving or taking of dowry at the time when deceased- Tara got married to the accused-respondent (husband).
There was no discussion between both the sides regarding dowry and that he gave whatever he wanted to give out of his own free will, in the marriage.

Chuni Lal vs Tejmaal And Ors (2024:Rj-Jd:41780-Db) on 27 September, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/61538477/
5 17.

entities.text: Chuni Lal vs Tejmaal And Ors (2024:Rj-Jd:41780-Db)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
This Court further observes that another pertinent element of the offence under Section 304B IPC is, "soon before her death she was subjected to cruelty or harassment by her husband or any [2024:RJ-JD:41780-DB] (10 of 15) [CRLA-336/1997] relative of her husband for, or in connection with, any demand for dowry".
17.1

At this juncture this Court is conscious of the judgment rendered by the Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Chabi Karmakar & Ors. v. State of West Bengal, (Criminal Appeal No. 1556 of 2013,
decided on 29.08.2024),

entities.text: Chabi Karmakar & Ors. v. State of West Bengal, (Criminal Appeal No. 1556 of 2013
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
relevant portion whereof is reproduced as follows:
"In paragraph 9 of Rajinder Singh (Supra), this Court had discussed the ingredients of Section 304B of IPC as follows:
9. The ingredients of the offence under Section 304-B IPC have been stated and restated in many judgments.

17.2. The Hon'ble Apex Court stated that merely an unnatural death of a woman in the matrimonial home within seven years of marriage will not be a sufficient ground to convict the accused under Sections 304B and 498A of IPC, unless the prosecution has been able to prove that the deceased,
soon before her death, was subjected to cruelty in connection with the demand of dowry. 17.3.

However, in the present factual matrix, from testimonies of the prosecution witnesses available on the record, i.e. of PW1, PW 4, PW6, PW7, it is clear that none of them was aware of any incident which might have occurred or any circumstances which might have existed between the time of the deceased leaving her [2024:RJ-JD:41780-DB] (11 of 15) [CRLA-336/1997] parents' house on 09.03.1995 and the date of her death on 01.04.1995, in her in-laws' house.
They have no evidence to show a close proximity between the cruelty/harassment for dowry and the death of the deceased.

17.4. In the present case as well, the prosecution has failed to prove the aforesaid element of Section 304-B IPC, as against the accused-respondents, beyond all reasonable doubts and in absence of the same, no presumption can be raised under Section 113-B of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, qua the accused- respondents.

18. This Court, therefore, observes that in absence of any direct evidence, the onus lies on the prosecution to establish a complete chain of circumstances, which could point towards one and only one conclusion which is the guilt of the accused and no other.

However, in the present factual Chuni Lal vs Tejmaal And Ors (2024:Rj-Jd:41780-Db) on 27 September, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/61538477/
6 matrix, the story of prosecution is knotted due to vitiated shreds of evidence and does not point only towards the guilt of the accused.

entities.text: Chuni Lal vs Tejmaal And Ors (2024:Rj-Jd:41780-Db)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 19. At this juncture, this Court deems it appropriate to reproduce the relevant portions of the judgments rendered by the Hon'ble Apex Court in the cases of Mallappa & Ors.
Vs. State of Karnataka (Criminal Appeal No. 1162/2011, decided on 12.02.2024) and Babu Sahebagouda Rudragoudar and Ors.

Vs. State of Karnataka (Criminal Appeal No. 985/2010, decided on 19.04.2024), as hereunder-:
Mallappa & Ors. (Supra):
"36.
Our criminal jurisprudence is essentially based on the promise that no innocent shall be condemned as guilty.

All [2024:RJ-JD:41780-DB] (12 of 15)
[CRLA-336/1997] the safeguards and the jurisprudential values of criminal law, are intended to prevent any failure of justice.
Babu Sahebagouda Rudragoudar and Ors.
(Supra):

"38. Further, in the case of H.D. Sundara & Ors. v. State of Karnataka (2023) 9 SCC 581 this Court summarized the principles governing the exercise of appellate jurisdiction while dealing with an appeal against acquittal under Section 378 of CrPC as follows:
Chuni Lal vs Tejmaal And Ors (2024:Rj-Jd:41780-Db) on 27 September, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/61538477/
7

entities.label: PRECEDENT

entities.text: Chuni Lal vs Tejmaal And Ors (2024:Rj-Jd:41780-Db)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The acquittal of the accused further strengthens the presumption of innocence;
8.2. The appellate court, while hearing an appeal against acquittal, is entitled to reappreciate the oral and documentary evidence;

8.3. The appellate court, while deciding an appeal against acquittal, after reappreciating the evidence, is required to consider whether the view taken by the trial [2024:RJ-JD:41780-DB] (13 of 15) [CRLA-336/1997] court is a possible view which could have been taken on the basis of the evidence on record;
8.4. If the view taken is a possible view, the appellate court cannot overturn the order of acquittal on the ground that another view was also possible; and 8.5.

The appellate court can interfere with the order of acquittal only if it comes to a finding that the only conclusion which can be recorded on the basis of the evidence on record was that the guilt of the accused was proved beyond a reasonable doubt and no other conclusion was possible."
39.

Thus, it is beyond the pale of doubt that the scope of interference by an appellate Court for reversing the judgment of acquittal recorded by the trial Court in favour of the accused has to be exercised within the four corners of the following principles: (a) That the judgment of acquittal suffers from patent perversity;
(b) That the same is based on a misreading/ omission to consider material evidence on record; (c)
That no two reasonable views are possible and only the view consistent with the guilt of the accused is possible from the evidence available on record."
20.

This Court further observes that the learned Trial Court passed the impugned judgment of acquittal qua the surviving accused- respondents under Sections 498A, 302/304 304B and 306 IPC,
which in the given circumstances, is justified in law, because as per the settled principles of law as laid down by the Hon'ble Apex Court in the aforementioned judgments, to the effect that the judgment of the Trial Court can be reversed by the Appellate Court only when it demonstrates an illegality, perversity or error of law or fact in arriving at such decision; but in the present case, the learned Trial Court, before passing the impugned judgment [2024:RJ-JD:41780-DB] (14 of 15)
[CRLA-336/1997] had examined each and every witness at a considerable length and duly analyzed the documents produced before it, coupled with examination of the oral as well as documentary evidence, and thus, the impugned judgment suffers from no perversity or error of law or fact, so as to warrant any interference by this Court in the instant appeal.
20.1.

Thus, in light of the factual matrix of the case and the evidences adduced showing a delay in the lodging of FIR, the absence of any other injury marks showing cruelty or previous marital discord and resultant possibility of concoction, along with no presentment of evidence by the prosecution to prove the charges levelled under Section 302 IPC, this Court observes that the prosecution has failed to establish a chain of circumstances which point only towards the guilt of the surviving accused- respondents and thereby has failed to satisfy the Panch-Sheel Test.

Chuni Lal vs Tejmaal And Ors (2024:Rj-Jd:41780-Db) on 27 September, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/61538477/
8 21.

entities.text: Chuni Lal vs Tejmaal And Ors (2024:Rj-Jd:41780-Db)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: This Court also observes that the scope of interference in the acquittal order passed by the learned Trial Court is very limited, and if the impugned judgment of the learned Trial Court demonstrates a legally plausible view, and that a mere possibility of a contrary view shall not justify the reversal of acquittal as held by the Hon'ble Apex Court in the aforementioned judgment.

Thus,
on that count also, the impugned judgment deserves no interference by this Court in the instant appeal.

22. Thus, in the light of the overall facts and the circumstances surrounding the case, the impugned judgment of acquittal dated 29.11.1996 passed by the learned Trial Court cannot be said to be [2024:RJ-JD:41780-DB] (15 of 15) [CRLA-336/1997] anything, which would call for intervention of this Court to reverse the same.

23. Thus, taking into consideration the aforesaid observations and looking into the factual matrix of the present case as well as in light of the aforementioned precedent laws, this Court does not find it a fit case warranting any interference by this Court.
24. Consequently, the present appeal as well as the present revision petition are dismissed.

24.1. However, keeping in view the provision of Section 437-A Cr.P.C. / Section 481 of Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, the surviving accused-respondents are directed to furnish a personal bond in a sum of Rs. 25,000/- each and a surety bond each in the like amount before the learned Trial Court, which shall be made effective for a period of six months, to the effect that in the event of filing Special Leave Petition against this judgment or for grant of leave, the surviving accused-respondents, on receipt of notice thereof, shall appear before the Hon'ble Supreme Court as and when they called upon to do so.
24.2. All pending applications stand disposed of.
Record of the learned Trial Court be sent back forthwith.
25. This Court is thankful to Ms.Shrestha Mathur, who has rendered her assistance as an Amicus Curiae, on behalf of the accused-respondents, in the present adjudication.
(MUNNURI LAXMAN),J (DR. PUSHPENDRA SINGH BHATI),J SKant/-
